summary: Specifies how one RTP session can carry streams of several media types, such as audio, video and text. The RTP specifications had restricted this, so the document updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 to allow it for applications that fit its stated applicability. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Usually audio goes in one pipe and video in another. This document says that in some cases it is fine to put both in the same pipe, which can make setting up calls simpler.

questions: can audio and video share one rtp session
can an ssrc change media type
subtitle: When audio, video and text may share one RTP session, and the rules that make it work.

tldr.problem: RTP was designed to carry each media type, such as audio and video, in its own RTP session on its own transport flow. Firewalls and address translators make it harder and harder to set up several flows.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8860 updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 so that several media types can share one RTP session in defined cases. Each media source keeps its own SSRC, payload types are unique across the whole session, and the session is signalled, for SDP with BUNDLE.
tldr.outcome: Applications that meet the applicability rules can use fewer transport flows. Others, with very different network or RTCP needs, are better off with separate sessions.

today: RFC 8860 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It is not obsoleted or updated by a later RFC in the unit metadata, and it updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551.

sections.title: Why One Session Instead of Several
sections.content:
RTP was designed to send different types of media in separate RTP sessions, which means separate transport-layer flows. A video conference might send audio and video on separate UDP ports. With network address/port translation, firewalls and other middleboxes, setting up several flows between two endpoints is getting harder.

RFC 8860 therefore updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 to allow multiple media types in a single RTP session in certain cases. It changes nothing about several streams of the same type, such as multiple audio streams. RFC 8108 clarifies that case.
sections.eli5: Calls used to need one pipe for sound and another for pictures. Pipes are getting hard to set up, so this document lets you share one pipe when it is safe.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
Using several transport flows has three costs listed in the RFC: more delay to establish a complete session, more state in middleboxes that can cause unexpected behaviour when their limits are reached, and a higher risk that some flows fail to be established, which stops the application from communicating.

Separate flows do make it easy to apply network QoS per flow. But many RTP applications do not use network QoS and do not want different treatment for audio, video or text, so they gain nothing from that structure.

RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 still prohibit sharing, because RTCP timing rules assume all flows in a session have broadly similar reporting and feedback needs, and some extensions make assumptions about SSRC use and RTCP reporting that do not fit mixed media types.
sections.eli5: Every extra pipe has to be opened through the building's security doors, and each one might get stuck. Fewer pipes means fewer chances for something to go wrong.

sections.title: Applicability: When You May Do This
sections.content:
The RFC says this has limited applicability. An application should meet these criteria:

  • Equal treatment of media: one session normally means similar network treatment for all media. Applications needing significantly different QoS or RTCP configuration should use separate sessions.
  • Compatible RTCP behaviour: the RTCP timing rules give one reporting interval for all participants, so flows with very different sending rates or feedback needs do not fit together.
  • Signalled support: the extensions are not compatible with unmodified RFC 3550 endpoints, so use needs signalling and mutual agreement by all participants.
  • Consistent multiparty support: in a multiparty session every participant must support multiple media types in one session. A gateway between separate-session and single-session endpoints is not possible in the general case, partly because SSRC values can collide when sessions are collapsed.
  • Limited payload type space: a session has a single 7-bit payload type space.
  • Avoiding incompatible extensions: some RTP and RTCP extensions rely on multiple sessions or report on one media type only.
sections.eli5: Sharing a pipe works when everyone is treated the same, everyone agrees to share, and nobody needs special rules. If sound and video need very different handling, keep them apart.

sections.title: The Rules for a Mixed-Media Session
sections.content:
RFC 3550 said each medium SHOULD be carried in a separate session, and that separate audio and video SHOULD NOT share one. RFC 3551 said payload types of different media types SHALL NOT be interleaved or multiplexed within a single session. RFC 8860 rewrites these sentences to add an exception: they hold unless the guidelines of RFC 8860 are followed and, for the first sentence, the applicability constraints are met.

The mechanics stay simple. Receivers split packets into RTP streams by SSRC, and then use the payload type to pick the decoder. The payload type is never used to tell streams apart.

  • An SSRC MUST NOT change its media type during its lifetime. It may switch between audio formats but not from audio to video.
  • Different SSRCs MUST be used for different media sources.
  • Payload types MUST be unique across all payload configurations in the session, whatever their media type.
  • With media of different rates, endpoints MUST follow the RTCP guidelines in Section 7 of RFC 8108.

The reason for one media type per SSRC is that each SSRC has its own timestamp and sequence number spaces. Sharing them would make it hard to detect packet loss or know the clock rate.
sections.eli5: Each speaker gets their own name tag (the SSRC) and keeps it for good. Each kind of message gets its own label number, so the listener knows whether to play sound or show pictures.

sections.title: Interaction with RTP Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three extensions and notes where mixed media affects them. Future extensions should consider and document any incompatibilities.

Retransmission (RFC 4588). In SSRC-multiplexed mode, with several original and retransmission streams, the receiver must associate them by heuristics, or use different payload types so that the signalled apt parameter links them. Session-multiplexed mode is unaffected, because the same SSRCs are reused in the retransmission session. In SDP this needs BUNDLE and FID groups, and each retransmitted source needs its own m= line in the retransmission session.

Generic FEC (RFC 5109). Sent as a separate stream, FEC goes in its own RTP session using the same SSRC as the original. It is RECOMMENDED to use the application/ulpfec media type for RFC 5109 and application/parityfec for RFC 2733. Per-media-type names such as audio/ulpfec are legal but NOT RECOMMENDED, because they waste payload types.

Redundant audio (RFC 2198). It works with mixed media, but each redundant encoding needs its own payload type. With FEC as a redundant encoding for each media type, this can rapidly exhaust the available payload type numbers.
sections.eli5: Add-on tricks like resending lost pieces or sending backup copies still work in a shared pipe. Some need extra care, and a few use up lots of label numbers.

sections.title: Signalling
sections.content:
Setting up a mixed-media session requires signalling that does four things:

  1. makes every participant aware that the session has multiple media types;
  2. makes payload types unique, with no overlap between media types;
  3. keeps session-level parameters consistent, for example the RTCP bandwidth modifiers, the trr-int parameter, the transport protocol, RTCP extensions and security parameters;
  4. reuses RTP and RTCP functions bound to a media type where possible rather than configuring several code points for the same thing.

With SDP, the BUNDLE extension (RFC 8843) is used to signal such sessions.
sections.eli5: Before sharing a pipe, everyone must agree out loud that they are doing it and that no two label numbers clash.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP has strong security mechanisms, and most are independent of media type. The thing to check is that the chosen mechanism works with all media types in the session.

One session generally means one security mechanism for all media, whereas separate sessions can be secured differently. If media types have different security needs, separate sessions may be required, which costs resources and session setup time. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If everything shares one pipe, everything gets the same lock. If sound and video need different locks, they need separate pipes.

items.title: Equal treatment
items.text: All media get similar network treatment.

items.title: Compatible RTCP
items.text: One RTCP interval must suit every flow.

items.title: Signalled support
items.text: All participants must agree to it.

items.title: No incompatible extensions
items.text: Avoid extensions that need several sessions.
